da-2026-2-da-17.approach: Write down the ridge objective: the penalty is $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = \lambda\sum_j w_j^2$. Recognising the L2 norm squared (versus the L1 norm of lasso) settles it immediately.

steps.title: Ridge objective
steps.body:
Ridge regression minimises the residual sum of squares plus an L2 penalty:
$$J(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - x_i^\top w\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2,\qquad \lambda \ge 0.$$
The penalty is $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ — the **sum of squared weights** (the intercept is usually not penalised).

steps.title: Why it shrinks towards zero
steps.body:
Setting $\nabla J = -2X^\top(y - Xw) + 2\lambda w = 0$ gives
$$\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.$$
With orthonormal features ($X^\top X = I$) this is $\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = \dfrac{\hat w_{\text{OLS}}}{1+\lambda}$: every coefficient is scaled down by the factor $\frac{1}{1+\lambda}$, smoothly towards $0$ but never exactly to $0$.

steps.title: Match with the options
steps.body: The penalised quantity is $\sum_j w_j^2$ → option **(A)**. $\sum_j |w_j|$ is the lasso (L1) penalty, and rank / condition number are not penalty terms at all.

answer.value: The **sum of squared weights** $\sum_j w_j^2$ — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: ridge adds $\lambda\sum_j w_j^2 = \lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ to the squared-error loss.
$\sum_j |w_j|$ is the L1 penalty of **lasso**, which can set weights exactly to zero; ridge only shrinks them.
The rank of $X$ is a property of the data, not of $w$, and is not penalised. (Ridge does make $X^\top X+\lambda I$ full rank, which may cause this confusion.)
Ridge improves the condition number of $X^\top X + \lambda I$ as a side effect, but the penalty term itself is on the weights, not on any condition number.

da-2026-2-da-17.shortcut: Ridge = L2 = squares; Lasso = L1 = absolute values.
pitfalls: Swapping ridge (L2, $\sum w_j^2$) and lasso (L1, $\sum\lvert w_j\rvert$).
Thinking ridge produces exact zeros (sparsity) — only L1 does that.
da-2026-2-da-17.verification: In the orthonormal case the ridge solution $\hat w_{\text{OLS}}/(1+\lambda)$ reproduces the OLS answer at $\lambda=0$ and tends to $0$ as $\lambda\to\infty$, as expected of a shrinkage penalty on $\sum w_j^2$.

da-2026-2-da-18.approach: Apply the convolution output-size formula $O = \lfloor (W - K + 2P)/S\rfloor + 1$ to the spatial dimensions; the depth 3 of the filter matches the input depth and only fixes the output depth.
da-2026-2-da-18.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Input $W\times H\times C$ | $32\times32\times3$ |
| Filter $K\times K\times C$ | $5\times5\times3$ |
| Stride $S$ | $1$ |
| Padding $P$ | $0$ |

steps.title: Output-size formula
steps.body:
Along each spatial axis the filter can be placed at positions $0, S, 2S, \dots$ as long as it fits inside the padded input of width $W+2P$:
$$O = \left\lfloor\frac{W - K + 2P}{S}\right\rfloor + 1.$$

steps.title: Substitute the numbers
steps.body:
$$O = \frac{32 - 5 + 2\cdot 0}{1} + 1 = \frac{27}{1} + 1 = 28.$$
The height is identical ($32\times32$ input, square filter), so the map is $28\times28$.

steps.title: Depth of the output
steps.body: The filter depth $3$ equals the input depth, so each filter collapses the 3 channels into one: one filter gives a $28\times28\times1$ map (with $F$ filters, $28\times28\times F$). The spatial size is **$28\times28$** → option (A).

Thinking the filter depth 3 changes the spatial size — it only matches the input channels.

da-2026-2-da-19.approach: Use the definition: $Q$ is orthogonal when its columns (equivalently rows) are orthonormal, i.e. $Q^\top Q = I$; for a square matrix this forces $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$ and hence $QQ^\top = I$ too. Then knock out each other option with a counterexample.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
Let $Q = [q_1 \;\cdots\; q_n]$. Entry $(i,j)$ of $Q^\top Q$ is $q_i^\top q_j$, so
$$Q^\top Q = I \iff q_i^\top q_j = \begin{cases}1 & i=j\\ 0 & i\ne j\end{cases},$$
i.e. the columns are orthonormal — this is the definition of an orthogonal matrix.

steps.body: For a square matrix, $Q^\top Q = I$ means $Q^\top$ is a left inverse, hence the (two-sided) inverse: $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$. Therefore $QQ^\top = QQ^{-1} = I$ as well. So $Q$ is orthogonal $\iff Q^\top Q = QQ^\top = I$ → option **(C)**.

Rotation by $90^\circ$, $R =  egin{bmatrix}0&-1\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, is orthogonal ($R^	op R = I$) but $R 
e R^	op$ and $R^2 = -I

e I$, so (A) is not sufficient. Finally $\det(Q^	op Q) = \det(Q)^2 = 1$ gives $\det Q = \pm1 
e 0$, contradicting (D).

da-2026-2-da-20.approach: For a Poisson variable the variance equals the mean, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$; then use $\operatorname{Var}(aX+b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$ — the shift $b$ does not change the spread.

steps.title: Variance of X
steps.body: For $X\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$. Here $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$.

steps.body:
For $Y = aX + b$: $Y - E[Y] = a\,(X - E[X])$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = E\big[a^2 (X-E[X])^2\big] = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).$$
The constant $b$ cancels.

$12 = 3\times4$ forgets to square the scale factor.
$41 = 9\times4+5$ squares correctly but wrongly adds the shift; constants do not affect variance.

Using $a$ instead of $a^2$.

da-2026-2-da-21.approach: Match the argument form $P,\; P\to Q \;\vdash\; Q$ ("affirming the antecedent") against the standard named rules; it is exactly modus ponens.

steps.title: The argument form
steps.body:
Premises $P$ and $P\to Q$; conclusion $Q$:
$$\frac{P \qquad P\to Q}{\therefore\; Q}$$
This is **modus ponens**.

steps.title: Check it is valid
steps.body:
| $P$ | $Q$ | $P\to Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | T |

The only row where both premises $P$ and $P\to Q$ are true is row 1, and there $Q$ is true — so the inference is valid.

steps.title: The other named rules
steps.body:
- Modus tollens: $\neg Q,\; P\to Q \vdash \neg P$.
- Hypothetical syllogism: $P\to Q,\; Q\to R \vdash P\to R$.
- Resolution: $A\lor B,\; \neg B\lor C \vdash A\lor C$ (works on clauses).

Only modus ponens has premises $P$, $P\to Q$ and conclusion $Q$ → option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: $P,\; P\to Q \vdash Q$ is the definition of modus ponens.
Modus tollens uses $\neg Q$ and $P\to Q$ to conclude $\neg P$ — it denies the consequent.

Resolution works on clauses ($A\lor B,\ \neg B\lor C \vdash A\lor C$). After rewriting $P\to Q$ as $\neg P\lor Q$ it could also yield $Q$, but the rule that derives $Q$ directly from $P$ and $P\to Q$ is modus ponens (resolution generalises it).
Hypothetical syllogism chains two implications into $P\to R$; it needs no fact $P$ and concludes an implication, not $Q$.

da-2026-2-da-21.shortcut: Ponens = "putting" the antecedent ($P$) to get $Q$; Tollens = "taking away" $Q$ to deny $P$.
pitfalls: Swapping modus ponens and modus tollens.
Confusing it with the invalid "affirming the consequent" ($Q,\ P\to Q \vdash P$).
da-2026-2-da-21.verification: Truth table: the single row with $P = $ T and $P\to Q = $ T has $Q = $ T, so the inference is valid.

da-2026-2-da-22.approach: A moving average needs, for every row, an aggregate over a sliding set of neighbouring rows without collapsing the rows — that is exactly what SQL window functions (`OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …)`) provide.

steps.title: What a moving average needs
steps.body: For each row (e.g. each day of each store) we want the average of that row and its previous few rows **in the same group, in time order**, while keeping one output row per input row. GROUP BY cannot do this — it collapses each group to a single row.

steps.title: The window clause
steps.body:
A window function attaches an aggregate to every row:

```sql
SELECT store, day, sales,
       AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY store
                        ORDER BY day
                        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma3
FROM daily_sales;
```

\`PARTITION BY\` splits rows into independent groups, \`ORDER BY\` orders them, and the frame (\`ROWS BETWEEN …\`) defines the rolling window → option **(A)**.

steps.title: Why the others do not fit
steps.body: \`GROUP BY ROLLUP\` adds subtotal/grand-total rows, \`HAVING\` filters groups after aggregation, and \`PIVOT\` turns row values into columns — none of them defines a per-row sliding window.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: the OVER clause with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and a ROWS/RANGE frame computes rolling aggregates such as moving averages.
ROLLUP is an OLAP extension of GROUP BY that adds hierarchical subtotals (e.g. per (region, city), per region, grand total); it collapses rows and has no notion of a sliding window.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 only filters groups produced by GROUP BY; it computes no rolling aggregate.
PIVOT … FOR … rotates distinct row values into columns (cross-tab); it does not define windows.

da-2026-2-da-22.shortcut: "Rolling / moving / running / rank within group" in SQL ⇒ window function ⇒ OVER(…).
pitfalls: Choosing ROLLUP because it is also an "OLAP" feature — it builds subtotals, not windows.
Forgetting that without ORDER BY and a frame, AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY …) gives the whole-partition average, not a moving one.
da-2026-2-da-22.verification: Window functions keep the row count unchanged (one ma3 value per row), which is what a moving-average series requires; every other option either collapses rows or reshapes columns.

da-2026-2-da-23.approach: Use the second-order Taylor expansion at a critical point: the change $f(x^*+h)-f(x^*)$ is governed by the quadratic form $\tfrac12 h^\top H h$, which is positive for every small $h\ne0$ exactly when $H$ is positive definite.

steps.title: Taylor expansion at the critical point
steps.body:
With $
abla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H = 
abla^2 f(x^*)$:
$$f(x^*+h) = f(x^*) + \underbrace{
abla f(x^*)^	op h}_{=0} + 	frac12\,h^	op H h + o(\lVert hVert^2).$$

steps.title: Positive definite gives a strict minimum
steps.body:
If $H \succ 0$, let $\mu>0$ be its smallest eigenvalue; then $h^\top H h \ge \mu\lVert h\rVert^2$, so
$$f(x^*+h) - f(x^*) \ge \tfrac{\mu}{2}\lVert h\rVert^2 + o(\lVert h\rVert^2) > 0$$
for all sufficiently small $h\ne 0$. Hence $x^*$ is a **strict local minimum** → option **(C)**.

steps.title: The other cases
steps.body:
- $H$ negative definite: $h^\top H h<0$ ⇒ strict local **maximum**.
- $H$ indefinite: increases along some directions, decreases along others ⇒ **saddle point** (e.g. $f = x^2 - y^2$ at the origin).
- $H$ singular: test is inconclusive — $x^4$, $-x^4$ and $x^3$ all have $f'(0)=f''(0)=0$ but give a minimum, a maximum and neither.

optionAnalysis.reason: Indefinite Hessian ⇒ saddle point (e.g. $x^2-y^2$ at $0$), not a minimum.
A singular Hessian makes the second-order test inconclusive ($x^4$ min, $-x^4$ max, $x^3$ neither); it cannot guarantee a strict minimum.
Correct: $h^\top H h>0$ for all $h\ne0$ makes $f$ rise in every direction from $x^*$.
Negative definite ⇒ strict local **maximum**.

da-2026-2-da-23.shortcut: Gradient zero + Hessian PD ⇒ min; ND ⇒ max; indefinite ⇒ saddle; semidefinite/singular ⇒ inconclusive.
pitfalls: Treating positive **semi**definite as sufficient — it is only necessary (e.g. $x^4$ vs $x^3$).
Mixing up the signs: negative definite gives a maximum.
da-2026-2-da-23.verification: 1-D check: $f(x) = x^2$ has $f'(0)=0$, $f''(0) = 2>0$ (a $1\times1$ PD Hessian) and a strict minimum at $0$; $f=-x^2$ (ND) has a maximum.

da-2026-2-da-24.approach: Find the minimum number of nodes $N(h)$ an AVL tree of height $h$ can have — the recurrence $N(h) = N(h-1)+N(h-2)+1$ is Fibonacci-like, so $n$ grows like $\varphi^h$ and the height is at most $\log_\varphi n \approx 1.44\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Sparsest AVL tree of height h
steps.body:
To get height $h$ with as few nodes as possible, the root has one subtree of height $h-1$ and the other of height $h-2$ (the balance condition allows a difference of at most 1), each itself sparsest:
$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1,\qquad N(0)=1,\; N(1)=2.$$

steps.title: Invert to bound the height
steps.body:
Since $F_k \approx \varphi^k/\sqrt5$ with $\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx1.618$, any AVL tree with $n$ nodes and height $h$ satisfies $n \ge N(h) \approx \varphi^{h+3}/\sqrt5 - 1$, so
$$h \lesssim \log_\varphi n = \frac{\log_2 n}{\log_2 \varphi} = \frac{\log_2 n}{0.694} \approx 1.44\log_2 n.$$
(Precisely, $h < 1.4405\log_2(n+2) - 0.3277$.) Worst-case height $\approx 1.44\log_2 n$ → option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: the Fibonacci-tree bound gives $h \le 1.44\log_2(n+2) - 0.328$.
$\Theta(n)$ is the worst case of an **unbalanced** BST (a chain); AVL rotations prevent it.
Too small: any binary tree with $n$ nodes has height at least $\log_2(n+1)-1 = \Omega(\log n)$, so $\Theta(\log\log n)$ is impossible.
Impossible for any tree: a tree with $n$ nodes has height at most $n-1$.

da-2026-2-da-24.shortcut: AVL worst height ≈ $1.44\log_2 n$; red-black ≤ $2\log_2(n+1)$; perfectly balanced ≈ $\log_2 n$.
pitfalls: Confusing the AVL bound with the unbalanced-BST worst case $\Theta(n)$.
Using $N(h) = 2N(h-1)+1$ (that is a complete tree, giving the best case, not the worst).
da-2026-2-da-24.verification: Numerical check: $N(6) = 33$ nodes reach height 6, and $1.4405\log_2(33+2) - 0.3277 = 1.4405\times5.13 - 0.33 \approx 7.06 > 6$, while $\log_2 33\approx5.04 < 6$ — so the sparsest AVL tree really is taller than $\log_2 n$ but within $1.44\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: $$\operatorname{Var}(3X+5) = 3^2 \times 4 = 9\times4 = 36 \;\to\; \text{option (A)}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: $3^2\times4 = 36$.
$17 = 3\times4+5$ applies the transformation to the variance as if it were the mean ($E[Y] = 17$ is the mean, not the variance).
$12 = 3\times4$ forgets to square the scale factor.
$41 = 9\times4+5$ squares correctly but wrongly adds the shift; constants do not affect variance.

pitfalls: Adding the constant 5 to the variance.
Using $a$ instead of $a^2$.
Note $Y$ itself is **not** Poisson (its variance 36 ≠ its mean 17).
da-2026-2-da-28.verification: Mean check: $E[Y] = 3\cdot4+5 = 17$, which is option B — confirming B is the "mean" distractor. Standard deviation of $Y$ is $3\sqrt4 = 6$, and $6^2 = 36$.

da-2026-2-da-29.approach: Match the argument form $P,\; P\to Q \;\vdash\; Q$ ("affirming the antecedent") against the standard named rules; it is exactly modus ponens.

steps.title: The argument form
steps.body:
Premises $P$ and $P\to Q$; conclusion $Q$:
$$\frac{P \qquad P\to Q}{\therefore\; Q}$$
This is **modus ponens**.

steps.title: Check it is valid
steps.body:
| $P$ | $Q$ | $P\to Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | T |

The only row where both premises $P$ and $P\to Q$ are true is row 1, and there $Q$ is true — so the inference is valid.

steps.title: The other named rules
steps.body:
- Modus tollens: $\neg Q,\; P\to Q \vdash \neg P$.
- Hypothetical syllogism: $P\to Q,\; Q\to R \vdash P\to R$.
- Resolution: $A\lor B,\; \neg B\lor C \vdash A\lor C$ (works on clauses).

Only modus ponens has premises $P$, $P\to Q$ and conclusion $Q$ → option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: $P,\; P\to Q \vdash Q$ is the definition of modus ponens.
Modus tollens uses $\neg Q$ and $P\to Q$ to conclude $\neg P$ — it denies the consequent.

Resolution works on clauses ($A\lor B,\ \neg B\lor C \vdash A\lor C$). After rewriting $P\to Q$ as $\neg P\lor Q$ it could also yield $Q$, but the rule that derives $Q$ directly from $P$ and $P\to Q$ is modus ponens (resolution generalises it).
Hypothetical syllogism chains two implications into $P\to R$; it needs no fact $P$ and concludes an implication, not $Q$.

da-2026-2-da-29.shortcut: Ponens = "putting" the antecedent ($P$) to get $Q$; Tollens = "taking away" $Q$ to deny $P$.
pitfalls: Swapping modus ponens and modus tollens.
Confusing it with the invalid "affirming the consequent" ($Q,\ P\to Q \vdash P$).
da-2026-2-da-29.verification: Truth table: the single row with $P = $ T and $P\to Q = $ T has $Q = $ T, so the inference is valid.
